name: Congo African Grey Parrot
intro: The Congo African Grey is a medium-sized, highly observant African parrot, recognised by its scalloped grey plumage, pale face and bright red tail. Its remarkable ability to learn sounds is only one part of a complex, long-term relationship.
size: About 33 cm long; approximately 400–550 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: Often several decades in captivity; plan for a long-term commitment rather than relying on a maximum-age figure.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: The Congo African Grey is the larger and paler of the two commonly recognised African grey forms. It has a charcoal-grey bill, pale facial skin, finely edged grey body feathers and a vivid red tail. Juvenile birds may have darker eyes that change as they mature. Appearance can help identify the form, but an individual bird’s history and identity should be confirmed independently when relevant.

In the wild this species is native to equatorial Africa, where it forages and travels in social groups. A companion bird retains strong sensory, social and exploratory needs; it is not simply a talking ornament.

sections.title: Temperament and social life
paragraphs: African Greys are often attentive and cautious observers. Many take time to feel secure with new people, objects or routines, and confidence varies substantially between individuals. Respecting body language and allowing choice helps build a more trusting relationship than expecting instant handling or affection.

A bird may form a close bond with one person, but should still learn to occupy itself and interact calmly with other household members. A predictable daily rhythm can be reassuring; sudden changes, prolonged isolation or pressure to interact may be difficult for some birds.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: An adult Congo is roughly 33 cm from beak to tail and commonly weighs around 400–550 g. These are planning ranges, not standards for assessing an individual bird; sex, build and condition affect weight. A suitably sized enclosure needs room for fully extended wings, climbing and movement, not merely enough floor space to perch.
Published lifespan figures differ, but companion African Greys may live for several decades. Consider future housing, care costs and a trusted contingency caregiver before making a commitment.

sections.title: Talking, intelligence and training
paragraphs: This species is celebrated for vocal mimicry and may learn words, household sounds or whistles. No bird is guaranteed to speak, use words meaningfully or stay quiet. Calls can be sharp and carry through a home, so consider neighbours and the normal sound level of daily life.

Greys are quick to investigate patterns and benefit from short, positive-reinforcement sessions. Teach voluntary step-up, stationing, recall in safe spaces and comfortable movement into a carrier at the bird’s pace. Foraging puzzles and learning new behaviours provide mental work; avoid punishment, which can undermine trust.

sections.title: Food, housing and enrichment
paragraphs: Build a balanced, species-appropriate diet around a suitable formulated food and varied fresh vegetables, with fruit and other treats offered thoughtfully. Do not assume a seed-only mix is complete or copy a rigid online recipe. An avian veterinarian can advise on an individual plan, transitions and monitoring body condition; avoid routine supplements without professional advice.

Provide a sturdy enclosure with varied, safe perches, room to climb and flap, and supervised time in a bird-safe area. Rotate shreddable materials, foraging opportunities and toys, checking them regularly for damage. Daily attention should include independent play as well as interaction.

sections.title: Who may suit this species?
paragraphs: A Congo Grey may suit an experienced or carefully prepared household able to offer patience, routine, daily mental activity and a long-term plan. It is not automatically a beginner bird because it is famous for speech. Families should teach children calm observation and adult-supervised boundaries; the parrot must always have a quiet retreat.

Before enquiring, ask about the individual bird’s age, established diet, handling preferences, routine and current availability. Confirm what ongoing support is offered, how a bird travels to its new home and whether your household can accommodate noise, moult, cleaning and changing needs. Individual species stock needs confirmation; a species page is not an availability promise.

name: Timneh Parrot
intro: The Timneh Parrot is a compact African grey with darker charcoal plumage, a maroon tail and a distinctive pale horn-coloured upper bill. It shares the group’s intelligence and need for thoughtful interaction, while each bird has its own character.
size: About 28–30 cm long; commonly around 275–375 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: Often several decades in captivity; plan carefully for a long-lived companion.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Timneh Parrots are smaller than Congo African Greys, with dark grey feathers, a maroon rather than bright-red tail and a pale upper mandible. Their natural range lies in West Africa. Taxonomy and naming have changed over time in reference works, but the accepted scientific name used here is Psittacus timneh.

The compact build does not make this a low-needs pet. Timnehs explore with their beaks, feet and voices, and need safe ways to climb, chew, forage and observe their surroundings. An individual’s markings alone should not replace reliable identification and care history.

sections.title: Personality and temperament
paragraphs: Many Timnehs are watchful, thoughtful birds that prefer to approach new people and situations gradually. Their confidence, handling preferences and sociability differ; avoid treating a general species description as a guarantee about one bird. Giving a parrot the option to move away is an important part of respectful interaction.

Like other companion parrots, a Timneh needs both social contact and opportunities to spend time independently. Build a predictable routine that includes calm interaction, rest and foraging. A strong preference for one familiar person can develop, so gentle positive experiences with the wider household can be useful.

sections.title: Size and lifespan
paragraphs: A Timneh is usually about 28–30 cm long and often weighs roughly 275–375 g. Published figures vary, and an individual’s healthy weight depends on its build and condition. Enclosure design should give the bird room to climb, stretch both wings and move between perches, with safe access to exercise beyond the cage.

This is a long-term companion, potentially living for several decades under human care. Life expectancy is not a promise for an individual. Consider who would care for the bird if your circumstances change, and include suitable veterinary care in long-term planning.

sections.title: Talking, vocalisation and learning
paragraphs: Timnehs can imitate sounds and some learn human words, but talking ability is individual and cannot be guaranteed. Their repertoire may include whistles, calls and familiar household noises. These sounds are part of parrot communication; decide whether your home can accommodate regular vocal activity before choosing one.

Their alertness makes them well suited to positive-reinforcement learning and varied enrichment. Teach practical skills in brief, low-pressure sessions, such as stepping onto a perch, entering a carrier and targeting a hand-held object. Let the bird choose to participate; persistence, punishment or forced handling are not good substitutes for trust.

sections.title: Diet, housing and daily activity
paragraphs: Offer a balanced diet with appropriate formulated food and a variety of fresh vegetables, using fruit and richer treats in proportion. Seed mixes alone are not a complete feeding plan. Ask an avian veterinarian about the bird’s existing diet and how to make changes safely for that individual; do not add supplements without professional advice.

Use a secure, roomy enclosure, varied perch sizes and safe materials to chew and investigate. Supervised exercise in a bird-safe area, simple foraging tasks and regular toy rotation help provide activity. Keep the layout and objects safe: inspect toys and remove damaged items before they become hazards.

sections.title: Suitability and questions before enquiry
paragraphs: A Timneh may suit people prepared to learn parrot body language and provide patient daily care over many years. Smaller size does not mean a low-maintenance pet. A busy household can work only if the bird has reliable interaction, rest and a safe retreat; young children need close adult supervision around any parrot.

Ask about the specific bird’s age, diet, social history, handling preferences and routine. Discuss what happens during introductions, transport and the first weeks at home, and confirm current individual availability directly. These educational notes do not confirm that this species is in stock.

name: Blue-and-gold Macaw
intro: The Blue-and-gold Macaw is a large South American parrot, striking in blue and yellow plumage and requiring far more than a spacious cage. Its strength, social nature and powerful voice make careful household preparation essential.
size: About 76–86 cm long including the tail; around 900–1,300 g, with variation.
lifespan: Several decades is a realistic planning horizon; longevity varies and is never guaranteed.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Blue-and-gold Macaws have a turquoise-blue back and wings, golden-yellow underparts, a greenish forehead and a long graduated tail. Bare white facial skin is patterned with dark feather lines. They are among the larger commonly kept macaws, and their beak can exert considerable force.

Native to parts of Central and South America, wild birds use large areas and remain active in social settings. A companion needs comparable opportunities to climb, manipulate objects and make choices. Their spectacular appearance should never distract from the extensive daily and long-term commitment.

sections.title: Personality and social needs
paragraphs: These macaws are often inquisitive, energetic and socially responsive, but there is no single dependable temperament for every bird. Their size means that excitement, fear or frustration can have serious consequences if interactions are poorly managed. Learn to notice posture, eye and feather changes, and give the bird room to disengage.

A macaw needs structured attention without being expected to remain constantly on a person. Encourage independent play and foraging as well as calm shared activities. Household members should follow consistent boundaries and never tease, startle or allow unsupervised child–bird contact.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: At roughly 76–86 cm from beak to tail, with a typical planning weight around 900–1,300 g, this is a very large parrot. Measurements vary. Its housing must withstand heavy use and give the bird space to move, stretch, climb and play; a small cage with occasional release is not a suitable plan.

Blue-and-gold Macaws can live for several decades. Lifespan depends on many factors and no figure predicts an individual’s life. Think through the bird’s future care if you move, change work patterns or cannot continue as its guardian.

sections.title: Calls, intelligence and training
paragraphs: Macaws are capable of loud contact calls that carry over distance. They may also imitate sounds, but speech is not assured. Consider neighbours, shared walls and the times a bird might call when household members are out; training cannot remove normal parrot vocal behaviour.

Their curiosity makes positive-reinforcement training valuable for practical cooperation, including stationing, carrier entry and safe movement between areas. Sessions should be short and rewarding. Provide puzzle feeders and robust, bird-safe materials to investigate. Strong beaks make careful toy selection and supervision essential.

sections.title: Nutrition, housing and exercise
paragraphs: Provide a balanced plan based on suitable formulated food and a varied selection of fresh vegetables, with fruit and energy-rich treats managed thoughtfully. A seed- or nut-heavy menu is not a suitable default. Ask an avian veterinarian to review the bird’s diet, condition and any changes rather than following a fixed ration online.

Plan for a large, secure enclosure and a genuinely spacious bird-safe area for supervised exercise. Strong perches, safe climbing structures and enrichment made for large parrots are important. Check regularly for worn fittings, splintering or swallowed parts, and allow quiet periods as well as activity.

sections.title: Suitability and ownership questions
paragraphs: This species is generally best considered by people with the room, time, confidence and resources for a powerful, noisy, long-lived parrot. Families need clear adult-led routines and safe separation when supervision is unavailable. It is not a sensible choice simply because a young bird appears affectionate or can be taught tricks.

Before enquiring, ask about this individual’s age, behaviour, feeding routine and experience with handling. Discuss safe accommodation, household noise tolerance, ongoing care and current availability. Species information is educational: it does not indicate that a Blue-and-gold Macaw is presently available.

name: Scarlet Macaw
intro: The Scarlet Macaw is a large, unmistakable parrot with red plumage, yellow wing panels and blue flight feathers. This intelligent, powerful bird needs extensive space, social engagement and enrichment throughout a long life.
size: About 81–96 cm long including the tail; roughly 900–1,500 g, with variation.
lifespan: Plan for several decades of care; lifespan estimates vary and are not guarantees.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Scarlet Macaws have vivid red body plumage, broad yellow and blue sections on the wings and a long tapered tail. Their bare facial skin has fine feather lines. They are large birds with a strong hooked bill, capable feet and substantial movement needs; proportions and colour can vary with age and individual.

In the wild they inhabit forests and other wooded landscapes in Central and South America. Their social lives and wide-ranging activity are a useful reminder that a companion Scarlet Macaw needs meaningful daily choices and stimulation, not just a visually impressive enclosure.

sections.title: Temperament and social life
paragraphs: Scarlet Macaws are often described as alert and expressive, but generalisations cannot predict a particular bird’s confidence or handling preferences. Their size calls for respect: a frightened or overexcited macaw can injure someone unintentionally. Give clear space, read body language and avoid forcing contact.

They require consistent social interaction and should also practise safe independent activity. Foraging, chewing and training can become shared routines without making the bird dependent on constant attention. In homes with children, an adult should manage every interaction and provide an undisturbed retreat.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: A Scarlet Macaw can measure about 81–96 cm from beak to tail and weigh roughly 900–1,500 g. These figures are broad; individual build differs. A roomy, durable enclosure and substantial bird-safe exercise space are essential. Consider doorways, furniture, perches and safe flight or climbing areas before bringing a large macaw home.

Several decades is an appropriate planning horizon, although longevity is variable. Make a realistic plan for ongoing care and a backup guardian. An affectionate young bird is still a long-term commitment, and its needs and behaviour may change as it matures.

sections.title: Vocalisation and learning
paragraphs: Scarlet Macaws can produce piercing calls, especially when communicating or responding to activity. They may copy sounds or develop a vocabulary, but neither talking nor quiet behaviour can be promised. A house or flat with close neighbours may not be suitable for a bird whose calls are part of normal behaviour.

Training with rewards helps teach useful everyday skills and gives an intelligent bird a focused activity. Work gradually on stepping to a perch, waiting at a station and entering a carrier. Offer robust puzzles and safe materials that can be explored with beak and feet, and replace damaged enrichment promptly.

sections.title: Diet, enclosure and exercise
paragraphs: A suitable feeding plan includes an appropriate formulated food and varied fresh vegetables, with fruit and richer treats offered in moderation. Nuts or seeds should not simply become the bulk of the diet. Have an avian veterinarian discuss the individual’s food, body condition and any proposed change; avoid prescriptive quantities without professional guidance.

Use secure accommodation designed for a very large parrot, strong fittings, varied perches and supervised time to exercise. The bird needs climbing, wing-stretching and foraging opportunities. Rotate safe enrichment and check the environment for chew damage, toxic materials and escape risks.

sections.title: Who may suit a Scarlet Macaw?
paragraphs: A Scarlet Macaw may suit a highly prepared household that understands large-parrot behaviour and can provide space, daily engagement and long-term resources. It is not generally a straightforward first parrot. Families should consider loud calls, powerful beak use, mess and the need for trained, adult-supervised handling.

Ask about the individual bird’s history, diet, temperament, training and normal daily schedule. Discuss enclosure and exercise arrangements, household noise and contingency care, and confirm current availability directly. This guide describes a species, not stock; individual birds and needs must be confirmed.

name: Galah Cockatoo
intro: The Galah, also called the rose-breasted cockatoo, is a recognisable pink-and-grey Australian parrot. It is lively and sociable, but its need for interaction, activity and a thoughtful routine is much greater than its moderate size suggests.
size: About 35 cm long; commonly around 270–350 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: Can live for many decades; use a long-term care plan rather than a guaranteed figure.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Galahs have a rose-pink face and chest, pale pink crest, grey back and wings, and a lighter underside to the wings. They are a medium-sized cockatoo with a mobile crest and strong bill. In Australia, the species is also known as the rose-breasted cockatoo and occupies a range of open habitats.

The playful impression made by a Galah should not obscure that it is a cockatoo: an intelligent, vocal bird with social needs and a powerful beak. A companion needs safe opportunities to climb, chew and forage, plus an environment that accommodates powder down and regular cleaning.

sections.title: Personality and social needs
paragraphs: Galahs are often active, curious and engaging, although individual confidence and preferred contact differ. They may seek attention and can become demanding if their day offers little to do. Set a predictable rhythm with interaction, independent play, rest and foraging rather than relying on continuous handling.

Positive, calm contact should respect the bird’s choices. Household members can learn consistent cues and boundaries, while children should only interact under close adult supervision. A safe retreat lets a Galah move away from noise and activity when it needs a pause.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: At about 35 cm long and commonly around 270–350 g, a Galah is smaller than many cockatoos but remains sturdy and active. A suitable enclosure should allow climbing, wing stretching and movement between perches. Plan safe supervised time outside it, not just a compact cage because the bird is not macaw-sized.

Galahs may live for many decades. Published estimates differ and an individual’s life cannot be predicted from a general range. Long-term plans should account for changing household circumstances, ongoing care and who could take responsibility if needed.

sections.title: Calls, intelligence and training
paragraphs: Galahs communicate with calls, whistles and sometimes learned sounds. A cockatoo’s voice can be penetrating, and no training plan can guarantee a quiet bird. Consider the sound levels acceptable to everyone at home and neighbours, particularly if the bird will spend time alone during the day.

Their curiosity supports reward-based training and enrichment. Practise simple skills such as target following, stepping onto a perch and settling at a station, using brief sessions. Foraging materials and safe objects to manipulate help channel activity. Avoid encouraging rough play with hands or reinforcing unsafe behaviours.

sections.title: Diet, housing and exercise
paragraphs: Offer suitable formulated food alongside a wide variety of fresh vegetables, with fruit and calorie-dense treats measured thoughtfully. A seed-heavy menu is not automatically balanced. Ask an avian veterinarian to consider the individual bird’s established diet and condition, and seek advice before making substantial changes or adding supplements.

Provide a secure, appropriately sized enclosure, varied perches and daily supervised movement in a bird-safe space. Cockatoos enjoy shredding and manipulating safe materials, so rotate enrichment and inspect it for damage. Galahs may produce powder down; consider room ventilation, cleaning and the household environment when planning.

sections.title: Suitability and questions to ask
paragraphs: A Galah may suit an engaged household ready for regular interaction, noise, cleaning and a long-lived companion. Smaller size does not make a cockatoo an easy starter pet. Consider whether the household can offer activity while also teaching the bird to settle and occupy itself safely.

Before enquiring, ask about a particular bird’s age, daily routine, diet, social behaviour and handling preferences. Discuss how to prepare its enclosure and home, and confirm whether an individual Galah is currently available. Species descriptions are educational and cannot confirm stock.

name: Umbrella Cockatoo
intro: The Umbrella Cockatoo is a large white cockatoo named for its dramatic, fan-shaped crest. Its social intelligence and expressive nature come with substantial demands for attention, space, noise management and long-term planning.
size: About 46 cm long; commonly around 500–700 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: Potentially several decades; plan for a long-lived bird without assuming a maximum age.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Umbrella Cockatoos are mostly white, with a broad rounded crest that fans open when the bird is excited, curious or alarmed. Yellow colouring appears beneath the wings and tail. They have a strong dark bill and a robust body, and need an environment built for a large, dexterous parrot.

The species is native to Indonesia’s northern Moluccan islands. As a companion it retains a need to climb, explore, chew and communicate. White plumage and an affectionate reputation should not be mistaken for a decorative or low-maintenance pet. Cockatoos also produce powder down, a household consideration.

sections.title: Temperament and social needs
paragraphs: Umbrella Cockatoos are often highly interactive and expressive, but each bird has preferences and limits. Constant close contact is not a sustainable care plan. Teach calm independent play from the start and provide a reliable routine that balances companionship, foraging and undisturbed rest.

A bird may use its beak when excited, uncertain or seeking space. Learn its signals and arrange handling around choice, not pressure. Adults should supervise all interactions with children, and every family member needs consistent guidance about boundaries and safe contact.

sections.title: Size and lifespan
paragraphs: An adult is roughly 46 cm long and commonly weighs about 500–700 g. These are broad reference ranges. A large, sturdy enclosure with room to climb and stretch is essential, along with a secure bird-safe area for supervised exercise. Beak strength and escape skills require robust fittings and thoughtful room preparation.

Umbrella Cockatoos can be long-lived, with a care horizon of several decades. No general lifespan figure guarantees an individual’s longevity. Consider future guardianship, changing circumstances and the ability to provide continuing daily care before committing.

sections.title: Vocalisation, intelligence and training
paragraphs: This cockatoo has a powerful voice and can make loud contact calls. Some individuals imitate sounds, but speech varies and should never be promised. Sound is a normal part of parrot communication; think carefully about neighbours and the household’s tolerance before choosing the species.

Intelligence and curiosity make positive-reinforcement training and enrichment important. Practise voluntary carrier entry, stepping to a perch and settling on a station in brief sessions. Offer safe foraging and chewing tasks. Without satisfying activity, a bird may redirect its energy into persistent calling or destructive chewing; meeting needs is more useful than punishment.

sections.title: Nutrition, housing and activity
paragraphs: Feed a balanced, suitable formulated diet with a variety of fresh vegetables and thoughtfully measured fruit and treats. Do not rely on seed mixes or high-fat treats as the main food. Discuss an individual feeding plan, body condition and diet transitions with an avian veterinarian; routine supplements should not be added without advice.

Provide spacious secure accommodation, varied perches, safe exercise and durable chewable enrichment. Rotate activities to encourage exploration and food-searching. Inspect toys and fittings often. Plan for powder down, cleaning and ventilation as part of choosing where the bird will spend time.

sections.title: Is an Umbrella Cockatoo a fit?
paragraphs: This species may fit a well-prepared home with time for daily social contact, independent enrichment, noise tolerance and substantial long-term resources. It is not generally an easy first parrot. The bird must not be expected to fill a person’s entire social life; a sustainable routine benefits both bird and household.

Ask about the individual’s history, handling, diet, vocal habits and daily schedule. Consider room, neighbours, cleaning, safe access to exercise and a plan for care if circumstances change. Confirm current individual availability directly: this educational profile is not a stock statement.

name: Blue-fronted Amazon Parrot
intro: The Blue-fronted Amazon is a medium-sized South American parrot whose green plumage is brightened by blue on the forehead and variable yellow facial markings. It is lively and vocal, and needs room, interaction and thoughtful boundaries.
size: About 35–38 cm long; roughly 350–500 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: Often several decades in captivity; estimates vary, so plan for long-term care.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Blue-fronted Amazons are predominantly green, with blue feathers on the forehead and yellow colouring that varies around the face and crown. Red and yellow accents can occur on the wings. Plumage can differ between birds, so the name describes a species rather than a single exact facial pattern.

The species’ native range includes parts of South America. It is an active, intelligent parrot that benefits from climbing, foraging and social observation. Its colourful appearance and reputation for talking do not indicate that every individual will be easy to handle or vocalise in the same way.

sections.title: Personality and social life
paragraphs: Blue-fronted Amazons are often confident, alert and communicative, but individual temperament varies. Some birds are comfortable with change; others need a slower introduction. Learn to read posture and other signals, and use consistent positive interactions rather than assuming a bird welcomes touch whenever approached.

Routine, exercise and purposeful interaction help structure the day. Birds may show changes in behaviour as they mature or during periods of hormonal activity, so owners should be ready to adapt management calmly. Provide independent toys and foraging alongside social time.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: An adult measures roughly 35–38 cm long and often weighs about 350–500 g. These are approximate ranges, not targets for every bird. Provide a secure enclosure with space to climb, stretch and move freely, plus supervised exercise in a bird-safe room.

A Blue-fronted Amazon may live for several decades. Individual lifespan varies and cannot be guaranteed. Include future care, routine veterinary attention and the possibility of a long commitment in your decision, not just the initial setup.

sections.title: Talking, calls and training
paragraphs: Many Amazons can imitate words, tunes or everyday noises, but no individual is guaranteed to talk. Their calls can be loud and sustained. A prospective owner should think about sound travelling through the home and how the household will respond without reinforcing unwanted patterns or expecting silence.

These birds can engage with training and problem-solving. Reward-based sessions can teach practical behaviours such as target following, stepping up by choice and entering a carrier. Foraging challenges and safe objects to manipulate offer additional mental work. Keep sessions calm, brief and suited to the bird’s interest.

sections.title: Food, housing and exercise
paragraphs: Offer an appropriate formulated food and a varied selection of fresh vegetables and other produce, keeping high-energy treats measured. Avoid making seeds the whole diet. Consult an avian veterinarian about the individual’s diet, body condition and any transition; exact food amounts should reflect the bird rather than an online formula.

Use a durable enclosure, different safe perch diameters and a bird-proof exercise area. Allow regular supervised movement and rotate foraging and chew enrichment. Check toys for damage, and ensure household plants, wires, windows and doors are managed safely before the bird explores.

sections.title: Suitability and enquiry
paragraphs: This Amazon may suit a household that can offer confident, respectful handling, daily engagement and a tolerance for strong vocal behaviour. It is not a suitable choice for someone who expects a quiet pet or guaranteed speech. Families should set clear boundaries and ensure adults manage contact with younger children.

Ask about the individual bird’s history, age, diet, routine and response to handling. Consider space, noise, enrichment, and long-term care. Confirm whether a particular Blue-fronted Amazon is currently available; this guide is not a claim of stock.

name: Yellow-naped Amazon Parrot
intro: The Yellow-naped Amazon is a robust Central American parrot named for its yellow nape. Known for an expressive voice and strong personality, it needs skilled, consistent handling and an environment ready for noise and activity.
size: About 35–38 cm long; approximately 450–600 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: A multi-decade commitment is possible; published estimates vary and are not guarantees.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Yellow-naped Amazons are mostly green, with a bright yellow patch at the nape that can become more noticeable as a bird matures. Blue may show on the forehead, with other yellow facial markings varying between individuals. Their sturdy body and hooked bill are typical of medium-to-large Amazons.

The species is native to Central America. A companion bird remains active, social and vocal. Its distinctive colour and reputation for mimicking songs are not a substitute for learning the needs and signals of the individual bird.

sections.title: Temperament and social needs
paragraphs: Yellow-naped Amazons are often described as bold and expressive, but there is no predictable temperament shared by every individual. They can be sensitive to handling, particularly when excited or uncertain. Respectful boundaries, patient observation and steady routines are important for safe interaction.

A bird needs daily engagement and opportunities to occupy itself, rather than constant attention from a single person. Maturity and breeding-related behaviour can influence some individuals, so plan for changing needs and seek professional behavioural support when challenges arise. Do not assume sex determines a bird’s personality.

sections.title: Size and longevity
paragraphs: This Amazon is generally around 35–38 cm long, with a broad typical weight range of roughly 450–600 g. Size varies, and weight alone is not a full measure of condition. A sturdy enclosure should allow climbing and wing stretching, with regular supervised movement in a safely prepared room.

The species can be long-lived, and a commitment spanning decades is possible. Estimates differ, so it is more prudent to plan for a substantial care horizon than to treat a single number as typical or guaranteed. Consider a contingency guardian and ongoing care costs.

sections.title: Voice, learning and behaviour
paragraphs: This species is notably vocal and some individuals can imitate speech, music or household sounds. Neither talking nor a manageable noise level is guaranteed. Loud calls may be part of normal communication, which makes a quiet flat or noise-sensitive household a poor assumption without careful consideration.

Use positive reinforcement to teach cooperative everyday skills, such as waiting on a perch and entering a travel carrier. Short training sessions, foraging games and safe puzzles give the bird constructive work. Consistent routines and reading body language matter more than trying to suppress normal vocal behaviour through punishment.

sections.title: Nutrition, housing and enrichment
paragraphs: A balanced diet should include appropriate formulated food and a variety of fresh vegetables, with fruit and rich treats considered in moderation. Avoid a seed-based menu as the default. An avian veterinarian can help assess the individual bird’s food, condition and any planned changes; do not use supplements without specific advice.

Provide secure housing with varied perches, safe exercise and enrichment suited to a strong beak. Daily activity should combine social contact, climbing and food-searching. Rotate and inspect toys, keep the room safe, and provide a calm resting area away from household traffic.

sections.title: Suitability and questions before enquiring
paragraphs: A Yellow-naped Amazon is best considered by people ready for an assertive, vocal parrot and able to offer consistent routines, meaningful activity and respectful handling. It is not an automatic beginner choice. Families need adult supervision, clear boundaries and a way to give the bird space when it prefers not to interact.

name: Green-cheeked Conure
intro: The Green-cheeked Conure is a small, agile South American parrot with a green body, greyish chest and maroon tail. Playful and curious by reputation, it still needs daily activity, companionship and careful attention to its individual signals.
size: About 25–26 cm long; around 60–80 g, with variation.
lifespan: Often around 20–30 years in captivity; individual lifespan varies.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Green-cheeked Conures have green upperparts, a grey or scalloped-looking chest, maroon tail and colourful accents around the head and wings. Captive colour mutations can alter appearance, but the species retains its compact build and active nature. It is native to parts of South America, where it lives among social groups.

A small body does not mean simple care. These conures need exercise, safe chewing, foraging and daily interaction. They are capable climbers and explorers, so a bird-safe room and careful supervision matter as much as cage furnishings.

sections.title: Personality and social life
paragraphs: Green-cheeked Conures are often playful and curious, and many enjoy close social contact. Each bird has its own handling preferences, confidence and energy level. Nipping can occur when a bird is overstimulated, frightened or communicating a boundary; observe signals instead of assuming every approach is an invitation.

They benefit from attention balanced with independent play. A steady routine, safe toys and varied foraging can support a busy bird without requiring constant physical contact. Any introductions to other pets or birds need careful separation and supervision, never an assumption that different species will safely share space.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: This small conure is typically about 25–26 cm long and around 60–80 g. Individual size and weight vary. Select an enclosure with safe bar spacing, usable room to climb and move, and enough space for varied perches and toys; provide supervised exercise outside it as well.

Green-cheeked Conures may live for roughly 20–30 years, although estimates differ and individual outcomes vary. Plan for a lasting relationship, ongoing care and a future guardian if needed; a small bird can still be a major life commitment.

sections.title: Vocalisation, intelligence and training
paragraphs: Compared with some larger conures, Green-cheeks are often described as less loud, but this is not a promise of quiet. They make calls, chatter and may learn a few sounds or words; talking ability varies. Meet the individual before deciding whether its normal voice suits your home.

These intelligent birds can enjoy short reward-based lessons, target following and carrier practice. Add simple foraging tasks and safe objects to manipulate. Keep training upbeat and avoid punishment or forced restraint. Consistency helps a small parrot understand household routines and builds useful cooperation.

sections.title: Food, housing and enrichment
paragraphs: Offer suitable formulated food alongside a variety of fresh vegetables, with fruit and seeds used thoughtfully. A seed-only mix is not a balanced default. Ask an avian veterinarian about a specific bird’s diet and any transition, especially if it has been eating a different food; do not rely on restrictive or prescriptive online menus.

Provide climbing opportunities, safe perches, shreddable enrichment and supervised out-of-enclosure activity. Choose toys appropriate to a small bird and inspect cords, attachments and damaged parts. Rotate items and hide small portions of appropriate food for searching to encourage natural exploration.

sections.title: Suitability and ownership questions
paragraphs: A Green-cheeked Conure may suit an attentive household that can provide daily social contact, exercise and training. It can be an engaging companion, but is not a maintenance-free starter pet. Families should supervise children, respect the bird’s signals and ensure the bird has a quiet area away from busy play.

Ask about age, diet, handling preferences, vocal habits and the bird’s current routine. Prepare safe flight or exercise space and a plan for care across many years. Confirm whether an individual Green-cheeked Conure is currently available; species information is not a stock confirmation.

name: Sun Conure
intro: The Sun Conure is a vivid, medium-small South American parrot with yellow, orange and green plumage. It is often highly social and energetic, but its piercing calls and need for engagement deserve serious thought before choosing one.
size: About 30 cm long; approximately 100–130 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: Often around 20–30 years in captivity; estimates and individual outcomes vary.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Sun Conures are known for bright yellow and orange plumage, green wing feathers and a long tapered tail. Young birds can show more green, with colour developing as they mature. They are native to northern South America and are active, social parrots rather than quiet cage birds.

Their brilliant colouring can draw attention, but suitability depends on ordinary daily realities: noise, interaction, exercise and long-term care. Provide safe opportunities to climb, investigate and forage, and allow the bird to retreat from activity when it chooses.

sections.title: Temperament and social needs
paragraphs: Sun Conures are frequently described as playful and people-oriented, yet each bird differs in confidence, affection and tolerance for handling. A social parrot still needs boundaries and independent activities. Interaction should follow the bird’s body language instead of assuming it wants to be held whenever someone is available.

They may make frequent contact calls, especially when excited or responding to household sounds. A predictable routine can help organise attention and quiet time, but does not eliminate calls. Families should teach children calm behaviour and maintain close adult supervision.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: An adult Sun Conure is about 30 cm long and often weighs roughly 100–130 g. Measurements vary between individuals. Use an enclosure with safe bar spacing and enough room to climb and move, with supervised exercise in a parrot-proof area each day.

A Sun Conure can be a companion for around 20–30 years, though published figures vary and do not predict any particular bird’s life. Consider future care, housing and a backup guardian, rather than thinking of a small parrot as a short-term pet.

sections.title: Voice, intelligence and training
paragraphs: The Sun Conure is well known for a loud, high-pitched call that may be challenging in close housing. Individual vocal patterns vary, but it should not be selected on an expectation of quiet. Talking may occur, though speech is not the defining trait and is never guaranteed.

Curiosity makes positive-reinforcement training useful. Teach practical skills such as target following, stepping to a perch and entering a carrier, then offer simple puzzles and food-search activities. Frequent short sessions are more effective than long demands. Avoid responding with punishment to normal parrot calls.

sections.title: Diet, housing and exercise
paragraphs: A balanced diet includes suitable formulated food and a range of fresh vegetables, with fruit and seed treats kept in perspective. Do not use an all-seed menu as a shortcut. An avian veterinarian can advise on an individual bird’s existing food, weight and any gradual changes; supplements should only be used with professional advice.

Provide climbing space, safe perches, chewable enrichment and daily supervised activity outside the enclosure. Rotate toys, check them for wear and use foraging to make part of the day engaging. Make windows, fans, doors, plants and other household hazards safe before allowing exploration.

sections.title: Suitability and questions before enquiry
paragraphs: This species may suit an active household that can accept a loud voice and offer regular social time, training and enrichment. It is not a fit for someone who needs a quiet companion or cannot supervise a busy bird. Consider close neighbours and the bird’s needs when everyone is away.

Ask about the individual’s age, diet, routine, noise patterns and handling preferences. Prepare safe exercise space and consider care over decades. Confirm current individual availability directly; the presence of this educational profile does not mean a Sun Conure is available.

name: Black-headed Caique
intro: The Black-headed Caique is a compact, boldly marked South American parrot with a black crown, orange-yellow collar and green wings. Its energetic curiosity brings plenty of activity, and demands safe play, supervision and patient training.
size: About 23 cm long; around 130–170 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: Often several decades; estimates differ, so plan for a long-term companion.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Black-headed Caiques have a dark cap, orange-yellow cheeks and throat, green wings and a white belly. Their short, stocky shape and lively movement distinguish them from longer-tailed parrots. They occur in northern South America and are adapted to active foraging and movement through forest environments.

A caique’s compact frame does not mean its energy can be contained in a small cage. It benefits from safe climbing, foot play, food searching and interaction. Their agility makes supervision important wherever they explore beyond an enclosure.

sections.title: Personality and social needs
paragraphs: Caiques are often described as exuberant, curious and physically playful. Individual energy and handling preferences still vary. A bird may wrestle with safe toys or investigate objects, but play should be structured so that it does not include rough contact with people or unsafe household items.

Regular social contact matters, alongside practice settling and playing independently. Introductions to other birds should be gradual, with separate secure spaces and close management. Do not assume a confident caique will automatically be compatible with another pet.

sections.title: Size and lifespan
paragraphs: Black-headed Caiques are around 23 cm long and often weigh roughly 130–170 g. As with all ranges, individual build differs. Enclosure bar spacing must be appropriate for a small parrot, while the interior should still allow climbing, hopping and movement among varied perches.

Caiques are long-lived companions, potentially requiring care for several decades. Exact expectations vary between references and individuals. Plan for long-term housing, routine care and a future caregiver if your circumstances change.

sections.title: Calls, intelligence and training
paragraphs: Caiques can be busy and vocal, with calls, whistles and contact sounds. Their volume and frequency depend on the individual and situation. Do not choose one based on a promise that small parrots are quiet or that a particular bird will talk.

Their curiosity can make reward-based learning fun and useful. Practise target training, calm stationing and voluntary carrier entry in short sessions. Puzzle feeders, supervised foot toys and safe foraging turn energy into problem-solving. Teach clear routines and avoid encouraging nipping or rough play for amusement.

sections.title: Diet, housing and exercise
paragraphs: Offer appropriate formulated food with a variety of fresh vegetables and other produce; use rich treats and seeds thoughtfully. A seed-only diet is not a balanced default. Consult an avian veterinarian about the individual’s current food, body condition and any transition rather than applying a fixed diet prescription.

Give the bird a secure enclosure with climbing opportunities, varied perches and safe materials to chew. Provide supervised exercise and rotate enrichment frequently to maintain interest. Caiques explore with their beaks and feet, so check toys, flooring and play areas for small hazards.

sections.title: Suitability and ownership questions
paragraphs: A Black-headed Caique may suit an active, attentive home that can channel its physical play and curious nature into safe routines. It needs more than occasional cuddles and may not suit a household looking for a calm, hands-off bird. Families need adults to supervise activity and teach children gentle boundaries.

Before enquiring, ask about age, current diet, daily routine, play style and handling preferences. Discuss safe exercise and interaction with other pets, plus current individual availability. This profile is species education, not confirmation that a Black-headed Caique is in stock.

name: White-bellied Caique
intro: The White-bellied Caique is a compact, energetic parrot with a pale belly, orange head and green wings. It needs generous opportunities for safe movement and discovery, balanced by calm routines and respect for individual boundaries.
size: About 23 cm long; roughly 130–170 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: A long-lived companion, potentially several decades; figures vary and are not guarantees.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: White-bellied Caiques have a white chest and belly, orange-yellow head and green upperparts. The name includes related regional forms and taxonomic treatments may differ between sources. The bird described here is Pionites leucogaster, a South American parrot with a compact, sturdy build.

Caiques are active birds that use feet and beak to investigate their surroundings. In a home, they need appropriate climbing and play opportunities, food-searching and safe objects to manipulate. Their small size does not remove the need for a carefully prepared environment.

sections.title: Personality and social needs
paragraphs: White-bellied Caiques are often lively, playful and inquisitive, but a species profile cannot predict the temperament of an individual. Some may enjoy physical games while others prefer observation or a slower approach. Let the bird’s signals guide contact and avoid rewarding rough play with hands.

Plan regular interaction as well as independent activities, quiet rest and routine. Caiques can be very busy, so predictable boundaries help make household life safer. Any time near children or other animals should be carefully supervised, with secure separate spaces available.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: A White-bellied Caique is generally about 23 cm long and may weigh around 130–170 g. Individual measurements vary. Choose suitable bar spacing and ensure the enclosure is still large enough for climbing, movement and perches. Regular supervised exercise outside the cage is important for activity and exploration.

A caique can be a commitment of several decades, although published lifespan ranges vary. Consider long-term housing and care and identify someone who could help if circumstances change. A small parrot is not necessarily a short-term commitment.

sections.title: Vocalisation, learning and training
paragraphs: Caiques communicate with calls and other vocal sounds; volume and frequency vary between birds. They should not be selected on the assumption that a smaller parrot is quiet. Some may copy sounds, but talking is neither a dependable trait nor the measure of a good companion.

Positive-reinforcement training offers both structure and mental exercise. Introduce short activities such as target following, waiting on a perch and entering a carrier. Provide foraging tasks and safe toys that encourage problem-solving. Clear routines and calm redirection are preferable to punishment or forced handling.

sections.title: Nutrition, housing and enrichment
paragraphs: A balanced menu uses suitable formulated food and a range of fresh vegetables, with fruit and richer treats offered thoughtfully. Avoid relying on seed mixes as the main food. An avian veterinarian can review the bird’s current diet and body condition and guide any transition; avoid supplements without specific professional direction.

Create a secure home with varied perches, safe climbing and suitable chew materials. Rotate enrichment to sustain interest and offer supervised activity in a bird-proofed area. Check small toys and attachment points frequently, since busy birds can damage materials as they explore.

sections.title: Suitability and questions before asking
paragraphs: A White-bellied Caique may suit people ready for an energetic, hands-on parrot that needs daily activity and careful supervision. It is not ideal for someone seeking an especially quiet or low-interaction pet. Families should provide calm adult-led interaction and let the bird withdraw when it has had enough.

Ask about the particular bird’s age, routine, diet, play and handling preferences. Think through exercise arrangements, household supervision and long-term care. Confirm current individual availability with the seller; this educational profile does not indicate stock.

name: Papuan Eclectus Parrot
intro: The Papuan Eclectus is a striking parrot from the New Guinea region, notable for vivid colour differences between males and females. Their plumage does not predict temperament: individuals need careful observation, a balanced routine and a considered nutrition plan.
size: About 35 cm long; approximately 350–500 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: Often several decades; published estimates vary and should be treated as planning guidance.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Papuan Eclectus Parrots show pronounced sexual dimorphism: adult males are predominantly green with orange on the bill, while females are chiefly red and purple with a dark bill. Current classifications distinguish the Papuan Eclectus, Eclectus polychloros, from the Moluccan Eclectus, Eclectus roratus. Older references may use the latter name for a broader Eclectus complex.

Papuan Eclectus Parrots occur in New Guinea and nearby areas, with geographic variation. Their distinctive colour is a biological difference, not a guide to a bird’s character, trainability or suitability. Verify the identity and background of an individual with reliable records where relevant.

sections.title: Temperament and social life
paragraphs: Eclectus Parrots are attentive and observant, but their behaviour depends on the individual, history and environment. Do not make sex-based temperament guarantees or assume that a male or female will be more affectionate, calm or suitable. Learn the bird’s signals and give it a choice about interaction.

A steady routine can provide useful structure while allowing appropriate social contact and independent activity. Provide places to retreat and engage in foraging. Changes in behaviour should be considered in context and discussed with a suitably qualified professional when concerns arise; colour alone never explains personality.

sections.title: Size and lifespan
paragraphs: Papuan Eclectus Parrots are around 35 cm long and often weigh approximately 350–500 g. These are broad ranges rather than targets. Provide a roomy enclosure with varied perches and climbing opportunities, plus supervised exercise in a safely prepared area.

They can live for many years and may require care over several decades. Lifespan estimates vary and are not a prediction for an individual bird. Consider long-term care arrangements, household changes and future guardianship before deciding.

sections.title: Calls, learning and training
paragraphs: Eclectus Parrots can make clear, loud calls and may imitate sounds, but each bird’s vocal behaviour differs. Speech is not guaranteed, and no companion parrot is reliably silent. Think about how calls might carry through your home and affect neighbours before choosing this species.

Use positive reinforcement to teach voluntary carrier entry, stationing and calm handling routines. Foraging and simple puzzle activities add mental stimulation. Short sessions and consistent cues work better than pressure. The bird should be allowed to pause or decline; training should increase cooperation, not override its boundaries.

sections.title: Diet, housing and enrichment
paragraphs: Eclectus nutrition deserves individual consideration. Offer a varied, balanced plan with appropriate formulated food and fresh produce, but do not adopt rigid dietary prescriptions or assume all birds need the same proportions. Discuss food choices, body condition and any supplements with an avian veterinarian; do not add supplements routinely without advice.

Provide a secure enclosure, safe perches, supervised exercise and regular foraging. Rotate appropriate chew and puzzle materials, checking for damage. A bird’s surroundings should support movement and choice as well as quiet rest, and its diet should be reviewed as its needs and circumstances change.

sections.title: Suitability and important questions
paragraphs: This species may suit a prepared owner willing to pay close attention to individual behaviour, nutrition and routine. It is not a good match for anyone expecting sex or appearance to predict an easy temperament. Families need calm boundaries, adult supervision and a safe place for the bird to withdraw.

Ask about the individual’s age, sex if known, background, daily routine, diet and social preferences. Clarify what support is available for settling in and confirm whether a particular bird is currently available. This page offers general education and does not imply stock.

name: Budgerigar
intro: The Budgerigar is a small Australian parakeet with a long tail, lively flock behaviour and an unexpectedly rich capacity for learning. Its modest size still calls for flight, companionship, suitable nutrition and daily enrichment.
size: About 18 cm long; typically around 30–40 g, depending on build and variety.
lifespan: Often around 7–12 years in captivity; individual lifespan varies.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Budgerigars are small, slender parakeets with a long tail and fine barring across the head and wings. Wild-type birds are green and yellow, while selective breeding has produced many colour varieties. The cere above the beak can help with sex identification, but appearance can be less clear in young birds and some colour forms.

Native to Australia, budgies are naturally social and active. They use flight, calls and close observation to interact with their surroundings. Captive birds need room to move, opportunities to forage and a safe social environment; their small size does not make companionship optional.

sections.title: Personality and social needs
paragraphs: Budgerigars are often curious, alert and communicative. Individuals may be more comfortable with people, other budgies or a mixture of social experiences. Allow a new bird time to settle and build trust gradually; chasing or grabbing can make handling frightening rather than familiar.

As flock-oriented birds, they need meaningful social contact. If kept alone, they require regular interaction and enrichment from their people; if housed with another budgie, monitor compatibility and provide enough resources. A companion does not remove the need for daily observation and care.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: A typical budgerigar measures about 18 cm from head to tail and often weighs around 30–40 g, although size varies with build and variety. A spacious enclosure should prioritise usable horizontal flight space, safe bar spacing and multiple perches rather than decorative clutter.

Many companion budgies live around 7–12 years, but an individual’s lifespan varies. Plan for care over years, including safe housing, companionship and access to an avian veterinarian. A small bird can still depend on its keeper every day.

sections.title: Chatter, talking and learning
paragraphs: Budgies often chatter, chirp and whistle throughout the day. Some learn to imitate words or sounds, but speech depends on the individual and is never guaranteed. Flock calls and lively conversation are normal behaviours, so consider whether their frequent vocal activity suits the home.

These intelligent small parrots can learn through patient, reward-based interaction. Offer target training, gentle step-up practice and simple foraging challenges. Speak softly, keep sessions short and stop if the bird appears uncomfortable. Learning is enrichment, not a test of whether the bird is tame or valuable.

sections.title: Diet, housing and exercise
paragraphs: Use a balanced species-appropriate diet, often based on suitable formulated food with a variety of fresh vegetables and some appropriate seed. Avoid relying entirely on a seed mix. Ask an avian veterinarian about the bird’s current diet, body condition and gradual transitions rather than following a one-size-fits-all ration.

Allow safe flight and movement in a bird-proofed space, with natural-looking perches, chewable materials and opportunities to search for food. Check bar spacing and toys carefully; small birds can become entangled in loose fibres or unsafe attachments. Keep the enclosure clean and provide undisturbed rest.

sections.title: Suitability and questions before choosing
paragraphs: Budgerigars can suit a range of households willing to provide daily care, but they are not disposable starter pets. Their social needs, noise and sensitivity deserve respect. Children should learn calm observation and interact only with an adult supervising, while the bird has somewhere quiet to retreat.

Ask about the bird’s age, diet, social history and comfort with handling. Consider whether you can provide a companion or regular interaction, safe flight space and ongoing care. Confirm individual availability directly; this guide does not imply a budgerigar is currently in stock.

name: Indian Ringneck Parakeet
intro: The Indian Ringneck is a long-tailed, medium-sized parakeet known for its alert nature and potential to learn sounds. It needs patient socialisation, regular flight and enrichment, and should not be chosen on assumptions about speech or tameness.
size: About 40 cm long including the tail; around 110–140 g, with variation.
lifespan: Often around 20–30 years in captivity; individual estimates vary.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Indian Ringnecks have a slender body, long pointed tail and strong red bill. Green is common in the wild-type form, and captive colour varieties are widely seen. Adult males typically develop a dark and rose-coloured neck ring; females and young birds may not show the same markings. Colour varieties and age can make visual sex identification uncertain.

The species belongs to the rose-ringed parakeet group and is native across parts of Africa and South Asia. Its nimble flight and active exploratory behaviour mean a home needs safe movement space as well as an enclosure.

sections.title: Personality and social life
paragraphs: Indian Ringnecks are often observant and independent, with individual differences in confidence and willingness to handle. Some go through periods of greater wariness as they mature. Patient, choice-based interaction is more helpful than assuming a bird should always accept hands or close contact.

They need daily social interaction and things to do when people are busy. A predictable routine, training and foraging can help structure time. Respect boundaries and let the bird retreat; children should never handle a parakeet without close adult supervision.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: An Indian Ringneck measures around 40 cm from head to tail, with the long tail contributing much of its length, and commonly weighs about 110–140 g. Figures vary. Give it room to climb and exercise, appropriate bar spacing and safe opportunities for supervised flight in a prepared space.
A companion may live around 20–30 years, but lifespan depends on the individual and care. Include a long-term plan, ongoing care and potential future guardianship in your decision.

sections.title: Vocalisation, talking and training
paragraphs: Ringnecks can produce loud calls and some individuals learn words or other sounds. Talking ability cannot be guaranteed, and frequent vocalisation may be challenging for neighbours. Consider sound levels and how much daily activity the bird will hear when the home is empty.

They are capable learners and can benefit from short reward-based sessions. Teach target following, voluntary step-up and carrier entry. Foraging and safe chew materials add independent mental activity. A bird that does not talk or accept handling is still a complete companion and should not be pressured to perform.

sections.title: Food, housing and exercise
paragraphs: Offer suitable formulated food and varied fresh vegetables, with fruit and seed treats used thoughtfully. A seed-only diet is not an adequate default. Have an avian veterinarian review an individual bird’s existing food and body condition, and guide any transition or supplement decisions.

Choose a secure enclosure with ample usable space, varied perches and climbing opportunities. Safe out-of-cage exercise, foraging and chewable enrichment help meet activity needs. Inspect toys for damage and secure windows, mirrors, fans and doors before supervised flight.

sections.title: Suitability and questions to ask
paragraphs: An Indian Ringneck may suit a patient household that accepts an active, independent bird and can provide exercise, enrichment and long-term daily care. It may not suit someone expecting a cuddly, immediately tame or reliably talking pet. Families should manage interactions calmly and consistently.

Ask about age, current diet, handling history, training and individual response to household activity. Prepare flight space and think through care over decades. Ask whether this particular bird is available now; a species guide is not an availability listing.

name: Peach-faced Lovebird
intro: The Peach-faced Lovebird is a small, compact African parrot with a peach-coloured face and lively, confident manner. It needs companionship, flight and engaging activity, while its strong personality calls for respectful handling and planning.
size: About 15–18 cm long; around 40–60 g, with individual variation.
lifespan: Often around 10–15 years in captivity, sometimes longer; individual outcomes vary.

sections.title: Overview and appearance
paragraphs: Peach-faced Lovebirds have a green body, peach-pink face and chest, and a short, rounded tail. Captive colour mutations can produce other combinations, but the species is identified by its compact form and characteristic face in the wild-type bird. It is native to south-western Africa.

Despite their small size, lovebirds are active parrots with strong bills and clear preferences. They need more than a tiny cage and a mirror: safe flight, social contact and opportunities to forage and chew are central to daily life.

sections.title: Temperament and social needs
paragraphs: Peach-faced Lovebirds are often energetic and bold, but handling style and sociability vary from bird to bird. Some are content to observe before approaching; others are more interactive. Slow trust-building and respect for signals make safer interactions than grabbing or persistent handling.

The common name does not mean a bird must live as a bonded pair, nor does keeping two guarantee companionship without conflict. Social arrangements require thought, observation and enough resources. A single bird needs meaningful daily interaction, while compatible birds still need individual attention and monitoring.

sections.title: Adult size and lifespan
paragraphs: Adults are generally around 15–18 cm long and weigh roughly 40–60 g. Their short proportions conceal a lively temperament. Enclosure bar spacing must prevent escape or injury, while providing enough room for movement, climbing and multiple perches. Daily supervised exercise in a secure area is valuable.

Many companion Peach-faced Lovebirds live around 10–15 years, and some may live longer; no single figure predicts an individual. Plan for long-term care, suitable companionship, routine observation and access to an avian veterinarian.

sections.title: Calls, learning and training
paragraphs: Lovebirds can be surprisingly loud for their size, with sharp calls and persistent chatter. Individual sound levels vary, but they should not be selected as a quiet alternative to larger parrots. Speech is not a typical guarantee; any learned sounds depend on the individual.

Short, positive-reinforcement sessions can build cooperation around stepping onto a perch, returning to the enclosure and entering a carrier. Offer simple foraging and safe objects to explore. Teach children calm observation and do not encourage biting or rough play as entertainment.

sections.title: Nutrition, housing and enrichment
paragraphs: A balanced diet should include appropriate formulated food and a varied selection of fresh vegetables, with seeds and fruit offered thoughtfully. Seed-only mixes are not a balanced plan. An avian veterinarian can discuss the individual’s existing food, body condition and gradual changes; supplements should not be given routinely without advice.

Provide secure, appropriately spaced bars, varied perches, safe shredding materials and supervised activity outside the cage. Rotate enrichment to maintain interest, and inspect cords and small attachments for hazards. Give the bird quiet rest as well as active play.

sections.title: Suitability and ownership questions
paragraphs: A Peach-faced Lovebird can suit people prepared for an alert, lively small parrot and willing to offer daily attention. It is not a hands-off decoration or automatically an easy pet for a child. Adults remain responsible for care, safe handling and any decisions about pairing or introductions.

Ask about age, diet, social history, handling and the bird’s routine. Think about safe exercise, companionship and long-term care. Confirm the availability of an individual bird directly; this page does not indicate that a Peach-faced Lovebird is in stock.
